300001:
Amends Saskatchewan's income tax rules to raise several personal tax credits and introduce a new home renovation tax credit starting in 2025.

  • Increases the basic personal, spousal and equivalent-to-spouse tax credit amounts gradually from 2025 through 2028, with further inflation adjustments after 2029
  • Creates a new home renovation tax credit for eligible home improvement expenses incurred from October 1, 2024 onward, up to $5,000 (or $6,000 for those turning 65)
  • Excludes certain expenses like furniture, appliances, hot tubs, and yard care from the home renovation tax credit
  • Raises the dependent child credit and senior supplementary credit amounts starting in 2025, with scheduled increases through 2028
  • Increases the Graduate Retention Program tax credit maximum from $20,000 to $24,000
  • Raises the income threshold for a related tax credit from $60,000 to $120,000 for 2025 and later years
  • Increases the Active Families Benefit to $300 per eligible child, or $400 for children eligible for the disability tax credit, starting in 2025
300002:
Repeals a section of The SaskEnergy Act and a section of the 2023 SaskEnergy carbon tax fairness amendment act.

  • Repeals section 7.5 of The SaskEnergy Act
  • Repeals section 4 of The SaskEnergy (Carbon Tax Fairness for Families) Amendment Act, 2023
  • Takes effect immediately upon receiving assent
300003:
Amends Saskatchewan's community safety law to add new powers for tackling nuisance properties, including rehabilitation and forfeiture orders.

  • Adds graffiti left unaddressed and storage or sale of stolen goods as grounds for specified use complaints
  • Creates a new process letting the director seek rehabilitation orders requiring owners to fix up nuisance properties within set timelines
  • Allows the director to seek forfeiture of nuisance properties to the Crown if owners fail to restore them
  • Lets the court order demolition of structures on nuisance properties and recover costs from the property owner
  • Protects certain interest holders, like banks and credit unions, from losing their registered interests when a property is forfeited
  • Creates investigator powers to enter, inspect and search properties suspected of being nuisance properties, with warrants where needed
  • Sets fines up to $10,000 for individuals and $25,000 for corporations on a first offence, rising for repeat offences, for violating orders under the new Part
300004:
Amends The Workers' Compensation Act, 2013 to update definitions, coverage rules, and appeal decision publication requirements.

  • Expands definitions of chiropractor, physician, psychiatrist and health care professional to include those practising outside Saskatchewan and recognized by their jurisdiction's licensing body
  • Creates a new category of 'out-of-province worker' covering workers residing in Canada, employed by a covered employer, and approved by the board
  • Allows a board member to finish hearing a case after their term ends, but not start new matters
  • Requires the board to publish appeal decisions along with reasons in a manner set by regulations
  • Removes the exclusion for forest fire scenes from a provision in section 28
  • Extends compensation rules to workers injured outside Saskatchewan if they are Saskatchewan residents, out-of-province workers, or usually work both inside and outside the province
  • Extends a provision about correctional facilities to include correctional facilities located in other jurisdictions
300005:
Amends The Saskatchewan Employment Act to update rules on work schedules, wages, leaves, gratuities, discriminatory action complaints and appeals.

  • Bans employers from withholding or deducting employee gratuities, except for approved pooling arrangements
  • Increases bereavement leave to 5 days per death or pregnancy loss, to be taken within 6 months
  • Extends critical illness/injury leave to up to 16 weeks and interpersonal violence leave up to 16 weeks
  • Raises the notice period for mass layoffs affecting 25 or more employees, up from 10
  • Creates a new referral and appeal process through the director of employment standards and adjudicators for discriminatory action complaints
  • Allows loss of pregnancy leave up to 20 weeks before the estimated birth date
  • Expands protections against discriminatory action to cover reporting offences, testifying in proceedings, and wage seizures
300006:
Prohibits carrying certain weapons like knives, swords, machetes, body armour and strong pepper spray in public urban spaces, with specific exceptions.

  • Bans possessing street weapons (knives, swords, machetes, body armour, explosives, strong pepper spray) in public places
  • Allows possession at home, while transporting to lawful storage, or for legitimate work, food preparation or wildlife protection reasons
  • Lets police seize and impound suspected street weapons without needing a criminal charge first
  • Sets rules for owners to request return of seized items within set time limits after charges are dropped or dismissed
  • Allows courts to order forfeiture to the Crown if a person is convicted or fails to claim the item in time
  • Creates offence with penalties up to a $5,000 fine, one year imprisonment, or both
  • Gives municipalities and First Nations the choice to opt into the Act, and their bylaws override this Act if they conflict
300007:
Changes rules on where Court of Appeal judges must live and increases the number of judges on the court.

  • Removes Humboldt from the definition of a northern centre
  • Increases the number of judges on the Court of Appeal from 6 to 7
  • Requires the chief justice and judges to normally reside in Regina
  • Allows the chief justice to permit a limited number of judges to live in Saskatoon instead
  • Lets a judge keep a Saskatoon residence once approved, unless the judge agrees to move
  • Allows a judge who leaves office to still deliver a decision on a case within 6 months
  • Gives the Lieutenant Governor in Council power to make regulations, including capping how many judges can live in Saskatoon
300008:
Amends Saskatchewan's child care law to add new facility types, change size limits, and set ownership and parent-involvement rules.

  • Creates a new licensed facility type called an alternative child care services centre
  • Creates a new category called preschool for care of up to 3 hours a day
  • Raises the maximum children in a group family child care home from 12 to 16
  • Restates family child care home limit as 8 children
  • Limits most applicants to having an interest in no more than one other facility
  • Requires licensed preschools to have a parent-majority board or a parent advisory committee
  • Allows the minister to exempt a licensee from parent involvement rules in cases of undue hardship
300009:
Updates how official documents under The Traffic Safety Act can be legally delivered or served to people.

  • Allows documents to be served personally, by ordinary or registered mail, or by other prescribed means
  • Adds a new option letting regulations set additional methods of serving documents
  • Lets regulations specify the day a document is deemed received when served by a prescribed method
  • Allows different service requirements to be set for different sections of the Act or regulations
  • Takes effect on a date set later by government order
300010:
Amends several Saskatchewan registry-related Acts to allow identity verification and digital signatures for public registries and to update related regulation-making powers.

  • Lets registrars verify the identity of people searching or filing documents in various public registries
  • Identity verification information stays out of the public registry but can be shared with police, RCMP or Canada Revenue Agency for investigations
  • Allows registrars to set rules for accepting digital signatures on documents filed in registries
  • Applies to corporate, business names, credit union, land surveys, land titles, co-operatives, partnership and personal property registries
  • Lets Cabinet make regulations on registry information use, including combining it with other data for new products and services
  • Repeals defamation-related sections and schedules in The Libel and Slander Act
  • Allows use of French and Indigenous language names for parties registered in the personal property registry
300011:
Allows registrars of the Co-operatives and Non-profit Corporations registries to verify users' identities and to authorize the use of digital signatures.

  • Lets the registrar verify the identity of people searching or submitting documents to the registry
  • Keeps identity verification information private and outside the public register
  • Allows sharing of identity verification information with police, RCMP or Canada Revenue Agency for investigations
  • Lets the registrar set rules for which digital signatures and technologies are acceptable for filings
  • Exempts registry digital signatures from The Electronic Information and Documents Act, 2000
  • Gives government power to make regulations on data access, disclosure and use of registry information
  • Applies the same identity verification and digital signature rules to both the Co-operatives Act and Non-profit Corporations Act
300012:
Authorizes the government to spend an additional $130,711,000 from the general revenue fund for public services in the 2024-2025 fiscal year.

  • Grants $130,711,000 total from the general revenue fund for extra spending not already covered
  • Allocates $97,165,000 to Corrections, Policing and Public Safety
  • Allocates $15,757,000 to Justice and Attorney General
  • Allocates $5,212,000 to Parks, Culture and Sport
  • Allocates $3,206,000 to the Public Service Commission
  • Allocates $9,371,000 to SaskBuilds and Procurement
  • Requires all spent money to be accounted for to the King, and the Act stays in force until October 31, 2025
300013:
Amends Saskatchewan's Income Tax Act to increase personal tax credits gradually through 2028, add a new fertility treatment tax credit, and create a rebate program for small business investment tax credits.

  • Gradually increases basic personal, spousal, equivalent-to-spouse, dependent child and senior supplementary tax credits by $500 each year from 2026 through 2028
  • Creates a one-time fertility treatment tax credit of up to $10,000, covering 50% of eligible fertility expenses, starting in the 2025 tax year
  • Excludes certain fertility expenses from the credit, such as travel costs and treatments received outside Saskatchewan
  • Establishes a new Small and Medium Enterprise (SME) Investment Tax Credit rebate program, capped at $140,000 per certificate and $4,000,000 in eligible investment per business
  • Sets rules for how businesses apply for the SME rebate, including deadlines, required documents, and repayment obligations if amounts are overpaid
  • Adds legal immunity for the minister and staff acting in good faith under the Act, and new confidentiality rules for taxpayer information
  • Limits eligibility for Commercial Innovation Incentive tax credit applications made after June 30, 2027
300014:
Amends The Power Corporation Act to raise the corporation's borrowing limit and expand its power to finance related entities and projects.

  • Confirms the corporation and its wholly owned subsidiaries act as agents of the Crown without needing to name the Crown in contracts
  • Declares all property, money and profits of the corporation and its subsidiaries are Crown property exempt from taxation
  • Allows the corporation to make loans, advances and guarantees to entities it controls, on terms it considers desirable
  • Allows the corporation, on direction of the Lieutenant Governor in Council, to also finance other entities involved in power generation facilities or related projects in Saskatchewan
  • Raises the corporation's borrowing limit from $10,000,000,000 to $14,000,000,000
  • Takes effect immediately upon receiving assent
300015:
Amends the Alcohol and Gaming Regulation Act to let the liquor authority set payment terms and charge interest on overdue alcohol sale accounts, and raises certain penalty amounts.

  • Allows the authority to establish payment terms for beverage alcohol sales transactions
  • Allows the authority to charge and collect interest on overdue beverage alcohol accounts
  • Makes unpaid amounts, including interest, a debt owed to the Crown
  • Allows debts to be recovered under The Financial Administration Act, 1993 or other lawful means
  • Raises a penalty amount under section 39.1 from $10,000 to $25,000
  • Raises a penalty amount under section 147.07 from $10,000 to $25,000
  • Sets the Act to come into force on a date set by the Lieutenant Governor in Council
300016:
Repeals a specific provincial sales tax exemption under The Provincial Sales Tax Act.

  • Removes clause 8(1)(oo.1) from The Provincial Sales Tax Act
  • The repealed clause previously provided a specific tax exemption
  • Change takes effect June 1, 2025
  • Bill does not specify what the exemption covered
300017:
Amends the Saskatchewan Commercial Innovation Incentive (Patent Box) Act to remove the economic eligibility test and extend a key time limit.

  • Removes the 'economic eligibility test' as a requirement for the tax rebate program
  • Extends a deadline referenced in the Act from 8 years to 10 years
  • Repeals sections 9 and 10 of the original Act
  • Removes a repealed eligibility requirement from the certification renewal process
  • Requires eligible corporations to notify the minister of any change affecting their continued eligibility for the tax rebate
  • Allows the minister to act if there are reasonable grounds to believe a corporation's circumstances have changed its eligibility
  • Most changes are retroactive to June 30, 2017, except the deadline extension which applies from the date of assent
300018:
Creates a unified legal framework governing how health professions in Saskatchewan are regulated, replacing separate acts for each profession with one common structure for colleges, discipline and licensing.

  • Replaces separate acts for professions like nurses, pharmacists, doctors, optometrists and others with one common regulatory law
  • Establishes colleges as corporations run by councils, including public appointees living in Saskatchewan
  • Sets common rules for registering and licensing health professionals and handling complaints against them
  • Creates a professional conduct committee and discipline committee to investigate and hear misconduct or incompetence complaints
  • Allows suspension, fines, conditions or licence cancellation for registrants found guilty of professional misconduct
  • Permits councils to waive registration requirements during a declared public health emergency
  • Allows amalgamation of multiple colleges into a single college and regulates health professional corporations

Written from the first part only of a very long text.
300019:
Updates the definitions of "medical practitioner" and "physician" in two other laws to align with the new Regulated Health Professions Act.

  • Changes the definition of duly qualified medical practitioner in The Legislation Act
  • Links that definition to a valid licence issued by the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Saskatchewan
  • Updates the definition of physician in The Vital Statistics Act, 2009 to match
  • Takes effect when a specific section of The Regulated Health Professions Act comes into force
300020:
Creates a tax credit program that gives investors a rebate for buying shares in registered small and medium-sized businesses or venture capital corporations in Saskatchewan.

  • Lets businesses apply to become a registered 'eligible business' until June 30, 2028, to raise equity capital
  • Allows eligible investors a tax rebate of up to 45% of their investment, capped at $500,000 per investor per year
  • Lets corporations register as venture capital corporations that invest pooled shareholder money into eligible businesses, capped at $225,000 in credits per year per corporation
  • Requires repayment of tax credits if shares are sold, redeemed or cancelled within 3 years of issue
  • Bans using the invested funds for prohibited purposes and bans investors from taking control of the business
  • Gives government inspectors power to audit records, enter premises and, with a warrant, search and seize evidence
  • Sets fines up to $10,000 for individuals and $100,000 for corporations for false statements or violations
300021:
Amends The Construction Codes Act to define derelict buildings and allow them to be demolished by fire under regulations.

  • Adds a definition of 'derelict building' based on future regulations
  • Allows the minister to create policies, strategies and programs to carry out the Act's purposes
  • Permits derelict buildings to be demolished by fire, following regulations
  • Gives authority to make specific regulations covering fire demolition of derelict buildings
  • Law takes effect on a date set by the Lieutenant Governor in Council
300022:
Amends The King's Bench Act to allow judges to attend approved meetings, conferences or seminars related to the administration of justice.

  • Adds a new section 2-8 to The King's Bench Act
  • Allows a judge to attend meetings, conferences or seminars
  • Requires approval from the chief justice for such attendance
  • Event must relate to the administration of justice
  • Ties this authorization to section 41 of the federal Judges Act
  • Takes effect immediately upon receiving assent
300023:
Authorizes the government to spend specific amounts of public money for the fiscal years ending March 31, 2025 and March 31, 2026.

  • Approves spending up to $923,955,000 for the fiscal year ending March 31, 2025
  • Approves spending up to $18,318,557,000 for the fiscal year ending March 31, 2026
  • Lists specific dollar amounts for each government department and agency in two schedules
  • Includes funding for health, education, agriculture, highways, social services and other departments
  • Sets aside $80,000,000 for lending and investing activities under Advanced Education
  • Requires that money be spent only for the purposes listed in the schedules
  • Stays in force until October 31, 2026
300024:
Requires Saskatchewan to recognize goods and services already approved in other Canadian provinces, territories or under federal rules, removing duplicate approval requirements.

  • Goods and services certified elsewhere in Canada must generally be treated as meeting Saskatchewan standards without extra fees or approvals
  • Workers certified in another province or territory are entitled to receive equivalent Saskatchewan certification if in good standing
  • Regulatory authorities must make their rules consistent with trade agreements and the mutual recognition principle
  • The minister can issue compliance orders forcing a regulatory authority to fix inconsistent rules within 60 days
  • Cabinet can make, amend or repeal regulations, or even override other Acts, to enforce trade consistency
  • Individuals who break the Act face fines up to $35,000, corporations up to $75,000
  • Courts cannot review the minister's compliance decisions and private lawsuits under this Act are prohibited
300025:
Expands Saskatchewan's fertility treatment tax credit so that both an individual and their cohabiting spouse can each claim it.

  • Allows both an individual and their cohabiting spouse to each claim the one-time fertility treatment tax credit
  • Lets eligible fertility expenses be counted over any 12-month period ending in the tax year, not just the tax year itself
  • Treats the tax credit amount as if it were tax already paid, reducing tax payable
  • Adds rules for deceased individuals, deeming them resident in Saskatchewan on the last day of the year they died
  • Sets limits on total credit claimed when separate tax returns are filed for a deceased person or estate
  • Caps the credit amount claimable if an individual or spouse becomes bankrupt during the year
  • Applies retroactively from January 1, 2025, once the bill receives assent
300026:
Repeals nearly 200 outdated public and private Saskatchewan statutes, most dating from the early 1900s, that are no longer needed.

  • Repeals two public Acts: The Companies Winding Up Act and The Saskatchewan Opportunities Corporation Act
  • Repeals about 198 private Acts incorporating old companies, churches, clubs, colleges and charities
  • Repeals many old city and town bylaw-confirmation Acts for places like Moose Jaw, Saskatoon, Regina and Yorkton
  • Repeals old tax exemption Acts for various religious and charitable organizations
  • Repeals two old Northwest Territories ordinances incorporating a club and a town
  • Most repeals take effect once the Act receives assent, except the repeal of the Companies Winding Up Act, which takes effect later by Cabinet order
300027:
Makes minor wording, translation, and cross-reference corrections across several Saskatchewan laws.

  • Corrects outdated references to dentists and pharmacists in gambling and liquor regulation law
  • Fixes an English typo, replacing 'Western Canada Lotteries Corporation' with 'Western Canada Lottery Corporation'
  • Removes an outdated reference to the federal Income Tax Act in the Constitutional Questions Act
  • Corrects a French spelling error in the Enforcement of Maintenance Orders Act
  • Clarifies that a reference to an 'order' in the Family Maintenance Act means a child support order
  • Replaces gendered pronouns like 'his or her' with neutral wording throughout the Vital Statistics Act
  • Updates references to renamed laws, such as The Saskatchewan Insurance Act becoming The Insurance Act
300028:
Amends The Public Libraries Act, 1996 to update terminology, modernize notice rules, and set out special provisions for library funding and governance in the City of Lloydminster.

  • Allows public notices to be published in online newspapers and sent by electronic mail, not just print and regular mail
  • Replaces references to the department with the ministry responsible for libraries
  • Adds Lloydminster-specific rules requiring library funding agreements between Saskatchewan, Alberta and the City of Lloydminster
  • States certain municipal library levy provisions do not apply to the City of Lloydminster
  • Requires interpretation of library funding rules to align with Lloydminster Charter and interprovincial agreements
  • Replaces the term Aboriginal with Indigenous throughout the Act, including in Part VIII heading
  • Removes an outdated definition clause and a repealed board duty clause
300029:
Amends Saskatchewan's alcohol law to let people bring their own beverage alcohol to certain permitted premises and special occasion events under set conditions.

  • Allows regulations to set extra situations where people may bring and consume their own alcohol at permitted premises
  • Permits special occasion permit holders to allow guests to bring their own beverage alcohol under regulated terms
  • Requires permittees and staff to demand age proof if a person appears to be a minor trying to possess or consume alcohol
  • Bans allowing a minor to keep or drink alcohol if they refuse or fail to prove their age
  • Extends existing liability and offence provisions to cover premises with a special occasion permit, not just permitted premises
  • Gives the Lieutenant Governor in Council power to set new rules on bringing alcohol to special occasion permit premises
  • Repeals a subsection of section 19.1 of the Act
300030:
Amends Saskatchewan's inter-jurisdictional support orders law to implement the Hague Convention on international recovery of child support and other family maintenance.

  • Adds new definitions like competent authority, contracting state, and convention to the law
  • Replaces references to telephone evidence with broader electronic means of communication
  • Limits ability to challenge registration of a foreign support order already registered in another Canadian province
  • Creates a new Part V.1 to implement the Hague Convention in Saskatchewan law
  • Designates a central authority responsible for handling convention applications and requests
  • Allows unsworn statements as evidence in convention-related applications
  • Adds the Hague Convention text as a Schedule to the Act

Written from the official explanatory notes (the bill itself is too long).
300031:
Replaces Saskatchewan's old libel law with a new Defamation Act setting out rules for notice, evidence, damages, privileges and online removal orders.

  • Requires anyone planning a defamation lawsuit to give the publisher 14 days written notice before suing
  • Lets courts order defendants to remove defamatory content, delete copies, or have it de-indexed from search engines and platforms
  • Allows a defendant's written apology to be used to reduce damages in certain cases
  • Introduces a single publication rule so republishing the same words does not restart the limitation period unless materially different
  • Permits consolidating multiple lawsuits from the same plaintiff over the same defamation into one action
  • Protects fair and accurate reports of public meetings, legislatures, courts, tribunals and peer-reviewed journal articles from liability unless malicious
  • Repeals the old Libel and Slander Act and updates related laws on the Ombudsman and Advocate for Children and Youth
300032:
Updates several Saskatchewan laws to replace the terms "libel" and "slander" with "defamation" to match the new Defamation Act.

  • Changes wording in the Jury Act, 1998 to use 'defamation' instead of 'libel, slander'
  • Changes wording in the Legislative Assembly Act, 2007 to use 'defamation' instead of 'libel'
  • Changes wording in the Small Claims Act, 2016 to use 'defamation' instead of 'libel, slander'
  • Takes effect on the same day the new Defamation Act's first section comes into force
300033:
Updates The Credit Union Act, 1998 to modernize membership withdrawal, termination and appeal procedures, record-keeping rules, and notice delivery methods.

  • Sets out clear rules for how members can voluntarily withdraw from a credit union, by oral or written notice
  • Allows a credit union to treat prolonged member inactivity as a withdrawal notice under conditions set by regulation
  • Creates a detailed process for the board to terminate a member's membership, including notice and hearing rights
  • Gives terminated members a right to appeal to the credit union's members or, in some cases, to the court
  • Requires credit unions to repay withdrawing or terminated members' shares, deposits and other amounts within regulated timeframes
  • Updates rules for record retention, destruction, and providing members paper copies of articles and bylaws
  • Changes allowed methods for serving legal notices, removing certified mail and adding regulation-prescribed methods
300034:
Expands the legal definition of interpersonal violence to include coercive control and cyberstalking.

  • Amends The Victims of Interpersonal Violence Act's definition of interpersonal violence
  • Adds a pattern of coercive or controlling behaviour as a form of interpersonal violence
  • Adds cyberstalking or online harassment as a form of interpersonal violence
  • Takes effect immediately upon receiving assent
300035:
Creates a new legal process allowing a minister to designate "subsurface development areas" letting operators explore for and produce minerals even when some mineral title owners cannot be located or have not consented.

  • Lets applicants apply to the minister to designate an area for mineral exploration, development or production
  • Requires the minister to notify affected mineral title owners and allow 30 days for written objections
  • Allows designation without owner consent after 5 years of unsuccessful search for the owner
  • Requires operators to pay a 'just and equitable share' of proceeds to unlocated or non-consenting titleholders, held by the Minister of Finance
  • Gives the Crown, ministers and officials immunity from lawsuits over decisions made under this new process
  • Clarifies that designation does not authorize entering or using surface lands, nor amount to expropriation
  • Updates rules on how the ministry can serve notices, including by mail, email or other prescribed means
300036:
Updates Saskatchewan's Change of Name Act to allow single names based on culture or religion and to modernize rules on name changes, consents, and fees.

  • Allows a person's name to be a single name determined by their culture or religion, subject to director approval
  • Requires written consent from a spouse before someone can apply to change that spouse's name
  • Replaces the term 'double surname' with 'surname consisting of more than one component' throughout the Act
  • Lets a person or their spouse choose just one part of a multi-part surname as their legal surname
  • Removes fees for altering vital statistics birth records when a name change occurs in another jurisdiction
  • Allows police force members to access vital statistics change-of-name information alongside existing officials
  • Requires that 'resident of Saskatchewan' and living in Canada be defined as being on a permanent basis
300037:
Updates Saskatchewan's vital statistics law, changing rules for naming children, appointing registrars, and handling birth, death and parentage records.

  • Sets new rules for how a child's surname is determined when parents agree, disagree, or when only one parent registers the birth
  • Allows a child to be given a single name based on cultural or religious practice with registrar approval
  • Lets the registrar add a parent's name to a birth record through joint applications or court orders
  • Allows funeral directors to submit death statements when no other authorized person is available
  • Permits the registrar to issue certificates to people who need them if satisfied there is no unlawful purpose
  • Lets the registrar order return of certificates that were misdirected or improperly obtained, making non-compliance an offence
  • Removes the word 'adult' from some rules about who can request certificates for children or siblings
300038:
Creates a legal framework requiring municipalities to acquire and service land for new schools when directed by the minister, with cost-sharing agreements and related amendments to planning law.

  • Requires municipalities to acquire serviced land for new schools when ordered by the minister
  • Requires school boards to formally identify when a new school is needed
  • Allows the minister to withhold municipal funding if a municipality fails to comply with an order
  • Requires contribution agreements between the minister, municipality and school board covering costs, timelines and land ownership
  • Excludes school-related land spending from a municipality's normal debt limit
  • Allows municipalities to use expropriation powers to acquire land for new schools
  • Lets municipalities require developers to dedicate extra land or pay fees for school sites, up to 12% for residential subdivisions
300039:
Amends The Education Act, 1995 so a specific land rule does not apply to school land acquired under The Building Schools Faster Act.

  • Adds an exception to section 350 of The Education Act, 1995
  • The exception applies to land acquired for new schools under The Building Schools Faster Act
  • That existing section no longer applies to such land acquisitions
  • The Act takes effect when section 1 of The Building Schools Faster Act comes into force
300040:
Amends Saskatchewan's animal protection law to create new enforcement roles, allow service delegation agreements, and establish an appeals process.

  • Allows the minister to delegate enforcement powers to outside organizations through administrative agreements lasting up to 5 years
  • Creates new positions of animal welfare inspector and chief officer to support enforcement and handle complaints
  • Requires humane euthanasia methods that cause minimal pain and result in rapid loss of sensibility and death
  • Lets veterinarians euthanize suffering animals without an owner present under certain conditions
  • Allows warrant applications by phone or electronic means, not just in person
  • Sets up an appeals board so people can challenge officers' decisions on animal seizure or expense recovery
  • Limits how much animal protection agencies can charge for expenses, with prescribed maximum schedules
300041:
Allows the Lieutenant Governor in Council to designate heritage days, weeks, and months recognizing the diverse peoples of Saskatchewan.

  • Lets the government designate specific days, weeks, or months as heritage days, weeks, or months
  • States the purpose is to recognize the strength Saskatchewan gains from its many peoples' heritages
  • Designations repeat annually unless the government sets other rules or repeals them by regulation
  • Does not apply to any day, week, or month already recognized under another law
  • Gives the government power to make regulations setting rules and dates for these designations
300042:
Amends The Saskatchewan Firearms Act to add inspection powers, medical reporting rules, firearm safety instructor designation, and compensation rules for firearms seized by federal law.

  • Allows firearms officers to inspect shooting clubs and ranges, including opening containers and copying records
  • Makes it an offence to obstruct or hinder a firearms inspection
  • Lets medical professionals report to authorities if a firearm licence holder has a dangerous medical condition
  • Protects medical professionals from lawsuits for good-faith reports and keeps reports confidential
  • Requires firearm safety instructors to be designated by the chief firearms officer, with penalties for unauthorized instruction
  • Deems a firearm seized if federal law removes an owner's right to own, possess or transfer it, triggering a federal compensation duty within 12 months
  • Lets the commissioner store, test, and arrange destruction or deactivation of firearms once compensation is paid
300043:
Amends The Cities Act, The Municipalities Act, and The Northern Municipalities Act, 2010 to modernize governance rules, reduce administrative burden, and update processes for assessments, appeals, and municipal boundary changes.

  • Allows councils to appoint a non-voting Indigenous advisor to council, similar to existing youth member provisions
  • Requires councils to offer orientation training to members after each general election
  • Extends the waiting period for resubmitting a rejected municipal boundary application from one year to three years
  • Requires cities and municipalities to publish financial statements, public accounts, minutes, and bylaws online starting September 1, 2027
  • Makes harassment under The Saskatchewan Employment Act a violation of a municipality's code of ethics
  • Protects municipal employees from reprisal for reporting wrongdoing to the Information and Privacy Commissioner
  • Removes authority to create new additional service areas and special service areas, replacing them with other legislative tools

Written from the official explanatory notes (the bill itself is too long), from the first part only of a very long text.
300044:
Replaces Saskatchewan's current co-operatives law with a new comprehensive Act governing how co-operatives are formed, financed, governed and dissolved.

  • Sets out rules for incorporating, naming, and governing co-operatives including one-vote-per-member and no-proxy-voting principles
  • Establishes requirements for shares, member loans, dividends, and distribution of surplus among members
  • Creates rules for directors, officers, meetings, financial disclosure, and member remedies against unfair treatment
  • Adds specific frameworks for consumer, housing, employment, health care, and multi-stakeholder co-operatives
  • Allows extraprovincial co-operatives to register and operate business in Saskatchewan
  • Provides for investigations, offences, and penalties for non-compliance with co-operative rules
  • Repeals the existing Co-operatives Act and a related Act, with consequential amendments to other statutes

Written from the first part only of a very long text.
300045:
Updates references to co-operatives law in about 20 other Saskatchewan statutes so they align with the new Co-operatives Act, 2025.

  • Replaces outdated references to older co-operatives laws with The Co-operatives Act, 2025 across many statutes
  • Makes corresponding changes to The Business Corporations Act, 2021, including rules on significant control registers and electronic signatures
  • Updates definitions such as co-operative, health care co-operative, and housing co-operative in various acts
  • Aligns The Financial and Consumer Affairs Authority of Saskatchewan Act with new Co-operatives Act powers and duties
  • Updates municipal, credit union, and financial regulation statutes to reference the new Act
  • Comes into force on the same day as The Co-operatives Act, 2025
300046:
Authorizes the government to spend $420,925,000 from the general revenue fund for public services for the fiscal year ending March 31, 2026.

  • Grants a total of $420,925,000 from the general revenue fund for the 2025-2026 fiscal year
  • Allocates $335,796,000 to Corrections, Policing and Public Safety
  • Allocates $17,129,000 to Government Relations
  • Allocates $68,000,000 to the Saskatchewan Research Council
  • Requires all spent money to be accounted for to the King
  • The Act takes effect on assent and stays in force until October 31, 2026
300047:
Creates new legal tools letting the Saskatchewan government and individuals sue drug traffickers to recover health and other costs caused by illicit drugs.

  • Lets the Government directly sue people who traffic, import or produce illicit drugs to recover health care and related costs
  • Allows the Government to claim costs on an aggregate, population-wide basis without identifying individual patients
  • Creates a new legal wrong (tort) letting individuals sue for injury, illness or death caused by illicit drugs
  • Sets up rebuttable legal presumptions that make it easier to prove a drug caused harm or costs
  • Lets courts assign liability among multiple defendants based on their share of risk contribution
  • Allows government appointments, grants and contracts to be cancelled if the person is convicted of a drug trafficking offence
  • Blocks lawsuits against the Government for cancelling such appointments, grants or agreements under this Act
300048:
Creates a legal system allowing authorities to detain and treat people with severe substance use disorders who are likely to cause serious harm, even without their consent.

  • Allows police, doctors or a judge's warrant to apprehend a person believed to have a severe substance use disorder and be at risk of causing harm
  • Requires an addiction assessment within 24 hours of admission to decide if a recovery order is needed
  • Creates a Compassionate Intervention Board with legal, medical and community members to hold hearings and issue orders
  • Lets a hearing panel issue in-patient orders (up to 6 weeks, renewable) detaining a person in a treatment centre for care
  • Lets a hearing panel issue out-patient orders (up to 6 months) requiring community-based addiction treatment and reporting
  • Allows courts to issue long-term in-patient orders of up to one year after 60+ days of prior detention
  • Guarantees patients a right to free legal counsel, hearings, reviews, and appeal to the Court of King's Bench

Written from the first part only of a very long text.
300049:
Amends Saskatchewan's Income Tax Act to increase personal, spousal, equivalent-to-spouse and disability-related tax credit amounts and adjust their annual indexing formulas through 2029.

  • Sets the basic personal tax credit amount to $20,381 for 2026, rising by $500 in 2027 and 2028, then indexed afterward
  • Increases spousal and equivalent-to-spouse credit calculations using similar $20,381 base amounts with $500 annual increases for 2026-2028
  • Raises the disability supplement amount to $8,358 per child for 2026, with $500 increases for 2027 and 2028
  • Doubles the maximum deduction for adoption, fertility and surrogacy-related expenses from $3,000 to $6,000
  • Sets the age credit amount at $2,569 for 2026, increasing by $500 in 2027 and 2028
  • Adjusts the child care credit formula for individuals under 18, setting the base amount at $14,266 for 2026
  • Changes deadlines and eligibility rules for the Saskatchewan Chemical Fertilizer Incentive rebate, including a 3-year application limit and new record-keeping requirements for eligible corporations
300050:
Gives the finance minister new powers to grant financial assistance for economic development and protects officials from lawsuits over good-faith actions under the Act.

  • Allows the minister to guide, coordinate and implement policies to develop and diversify Saskatchewan's economy
  • Permits the minister to give grants or similar financial assistance to people, organizations, businesses or First Nations inside or outside Saskatchewan
  • Restricts such financial assistance to programs and conditions set out in regulations
  • Shields the Crown, the minister and Ministry of Finance employees from lawsuits for good-faith actions under the Act
  • Allows regulations on financial assistance to apply retroactively, but not before the start of the calendar year of payment
  • Takes effect immediately upon receiving assent
300051:
Amends Saskatchewan's corporate capital tax rules to change tax rates for financial institutions, Crown corporations and other corporations, mostly effective April 1, 2026.

  • Increases the capital tax rate for most financial institutions from 4.0% to 6.0% starting April 1, 2026
  • Reduces small financial institutions' tax rate from 0.7% to 0.0% starting April 1, 2026
  • Cuts designated Crown corporations' tax rate in stages, reaching 0.0% by April 1, 2027
  • Ends the telecommunications Crown corporation's capital tax for fiscal years starting on or after April 1, 2027
  • Keeps the general corporate capital tax rate at 0.0%, continuing existing policy
  • Updates deduction formulas for capital used outside Saskatchewan to match new tax rates
  • Applies retroactively as if in force from April 1, 2026, despite coming into force on assent
300052:
Allows the government to charge application fees for permits under The Heritage Property Act.

  • Lets the minister require an application form and a fee, if any, set by regulation
  • Gives the government power to make regulations prescribing permit application fees
  • Allows those fee regulations to apply retroactively to a date no earlier than April 1, 2026
  • Makes the whole Act itself retroactive to April 1, 2026, once it receives assent
300053:
Extends deadlines for the Saskatchewan Chemical Fertilizer Incentive program and adjusts related eligibility and record-keeping rules.

  • Pushes the program's eligibility date from January 1, 2027 to January 1, 2032
  • Sets a new deadline of December 31, 2034 for applications for an SCFI eligibility certificate
  • Requires each SCFI eligibility certificate to state the taxation year it covers
  • Bars issuing any SCFI eligibility certificate for a taxation year after December 31, 2034
  • Removes a condition that previously limited who could be an eligible applicant
  • Updates recordkeeping rules to cover both conditional approvals and eligibility certificates
  • Repeals section 20, with some changes applied retroactively back to July 17, 2020
300054:
Overhauls rules for inmate segregation, transfers and discipline in Saskatchewan correctional facilities, adding time limits and independent review.

  • Renames 'community correctional' facilities as 'reduced custody' facilities throughout the Act
  • Limits administrative segregation to a maximum of 15 consecutive days
  • Requires written reasons for segregation within 12 hours and access to a lawyer
  • Creates independent review adjudicators, appointed for up to 4 years, to review segregation cases
  • Requires a daily health care assessment for any inmate in segregation
  • Sets new rules and maximum sanctions for minor and major inmate disciplinary offences, including fines up to $200 and disciplinary segregation up to 10 days
  • Allows temporary confinement of an inmate for a prescribed number of hours if needed for facility security or safety
300055:
Strengthens enforcement powers against unauthorized medical practice and raises penalties under The Medical Profession Act and The Regulated Health Professions Act.

  • Bans practising or claiming to practise medicine, podiatric surgery, or as a physician assistant without proper registration or licence
  • Lets courts issue injunctions and order people to hand over information or answer questions during investigations
  • Raises fines for individuals to up to $25,000 for a first offence and $50,000 for repeat offences
  • Raises fines for corporations to up to $50,000 for a first offence and $100,000 for repeat offences
  • Allows officers or directors of an offending corporation to be personally found guilty and fined
  • Sets a 2-year limit to start prosecutions after a violation is discovered, with a 1-year transition rule
  • Also raises fines and adds similar injunction and information-order powers under The Regulated Health Professions Act
300056:
Creates a new office of "associate judge" within the Court of King's Bench, setting out their appointment, powers, pay and discipline process.

  • Allows the Lieutenant Governor in Council to appoint associate judges with legal or judicial experience
  • Gives associate judges most of the same powers as judges, except for certain criminal, liberty and contempt matters
  • Requires associate judges to retire at age 70 and allows appointment of relief associate judges up to age 75
  • Sets up a commission to recommend associate judges' salaries, pensions and benefits, reviewed every four years
  • Establishes an associate judges review council to investigate complaints of misconduct or incapacity
  • Allows the council to suspend, reprimand, or recommend removal of an associate judge after a hearing
  • Lets an associate judge's oath, residence and restrictions on outside work be set similarly to those of judges
300057:
Amends the Information Services Corporation Act to update restrictions on transferring ISC's assets and intellectual property, revise the golden share rules, and reduce government-appointed board members.

  • Adds protection against transferring ISC intellectual property outside Saskatchewan if it is needed for existing 2023 service agreements
  • Adds protection against transferring assets or functions that would delay ISC meeting its 2023 agreement commitments
  • Repeals several existing clauses and Part III of the Act, removing certain provisions
  • Allows the golden share to be acquired by the Crown Investments Corporation under a business arrangement plan, keeping the same rights and terms
  • Reduces the number of board members the Lieutenant Governor in Council may appoint annually to 2 persons
  • Lets current government-appointed board members beyond the new 2-person limit keep their seats until the next annual general meeting
  • Changes regulation-making powers regarding notice of director appointments
300058:
Sets central standard time as the official time for Saskatchewan while allowing designated border areas to follow a different time zone.

  • Establishes central standard time (UTC-6) as the standard time observed in Saskatchewan
  • Allows the minister to create time option areas near the provincial border that follow a neighbouring jurisdiction's time
  • Time option areas can use UTC-5, UTC-6 or UTC-7, for all or part of the year
  • Requires municipal requests or government consultation with municipalities and First Nations before creating a time option area
  • Requires public notice at least 30 days before a new time option area takes effect
  • Gives this Act priority over other laws, bylaws and orders, including Lloydminster's city charter
  • Repeals the former Time Act and updates a reference in The Election Act, 1996
300059: Too short or too technical for an honest summary: see the official text.
300060:
Authorizes government spending of $654,878,000 for the 2025-26 fiscal year and $18,958,410,000 for the 2026-27 fiscal year from the general revenue fund.

  • Grants $654,878,000 from the general revenue fund for the fiscal year ending March 31, 2026
  • Grants $18,958,410,000 from the general revenue fund for the fiscal year ending March 31, 2027
  • Lists specific spending amounts for each government department and agency in two schedules
  • Largest 2026-27 allocations go to Health ($8,478,701,000) and Education ($3,144,332,000)
  • Includes $80,000,000 for lending and investing activities under Advanced Education
  • Requires funds be spent only for purposes set out in the schedules and detailed estimates
  • Bill stays in force until October 31, 2027
300601:
Declares the month of April as Sikh Heritage Month in Saskatchewan.

  • Proclaims April each year as Sikh Heritage Month
  • Recognizes Sikh Canadians' contributions to Saskatchewan's social, economic, political and cultural life
  • Notes April includes Vaisakhi celebrations and the creation of the Khalsa Panth
  • Aims to support Sikh heritage, art and culture in Saskatchewan
  • Comes into force upon Assent
300602:
Establishes a monthly "Buy Local Day" to encourage people to support Saskatchewan-owned businesses, suppliers and services.

  • Declares the first Saturday of every month as Buy Local Day
  • Defines a local business as one owned and operated by a Saskatchewan resident or a Saskatchewan-based co-operative
  • States the purpose is to promote the value of local businesses to the economy and communities
  • Encourages Saskatchewan residents to patronize local businesses, suppliers and services
  • Comes into force immediately upon assent
300603:
Declares September of each year as Ukrainian Heritage Month in Saskatchewan.

  • Officially proclaims September as Ukrainian Heritage Month every year
  • Recognizes over 160,000 Saskatchewanians of Ukrainian heritage in the province
  • Marks September 7th as the anniversary of the first Ukrainians arriving in Canada
  • Affirms Ukraine's right to be an independent and sovereign country
  • Comes into force immediately upon receiving assent
300604:
Amends Saskatchewan's referendum law to prevent the government from initiating a vote on seceding from Canada and to raise the petition threshold for such a vote.

  • Bars the Government, Lieutenant Governor in Council, or Legislative Assembly from starting a plebiscite or referendum on Saskatchewan leaving Canada
  • Requires any citizen petition for a secession plebiscite to be signed by at least 30% of electors
  • This raises the signature threshold above the normal rule for petitions under the Act
  • Adds a new section 2.1 to The Referendum and Plebiscite Act
  • Takes effect immediately upon receiving Assent
300605:
Requires Saskatchewan to recognize goods, services and certifications approved in other Canadian provinces or territories that have similar mutual recognition laws.

  • Applies to goods and services from other provinces or territories with similar reciprocal legislation
  • Goods approved elsewhere are treated as meeting Saskatchewan standards, with no extra fees or testing
  • Services licensed or certified elsewhere must be recognized in Saskatchewan without extra approval requirements
  • Workers with equivalent certification from a reciprocating jurisdiction must be granted Saskatchewan certification if in good standing
  • Does not apply to Crown corporations, regulated professions under labour mobility law, workplace safety rules, or government procurement
  • Allows exemptions by regulation for specific entities, goods, services or occupations
  • Bars most lawsuits against the government based solely on this Act, except as allowed under the Canadian Free Trade Agreement
300606:
Requires the health minister to publicly announce any hospital emergency room closure within one hour of its approval.

  • Minister must publish emergency room closure information via website or other electronic means
  • Public notice must be made within one hour of the provincial health authority approving a closure
  • Ministry must use existing resources to publicize this information
  • Costs of publicizing closures cannot be paid from the General Revenue Fund
  • The amendment takes effect on the date the bill receives assent
300607:
Requires the government to consult the Fransaskois community about historical and current challenges and report findings within a set timeline.

  • Officially recognizes the Assemblée communautaire fransaskoise as the provincial representative organization of the Fransaskois community
  • Requires Ministers to launch a Fransaskois consultation initiative within six months of the Act passing
  • Directs interviews with Fransaskois students, parents, and elders on historical and current challenges
  • Requires consultations to include Métis, First Nations Francophones, immigrants, and rural and urban families
  • Requires a public report to the Legislative Assembly within one year of consultations starting
  • Report must include key issues, recommendations, and possible legislative or policy changes
  • Act comes into force immediately upon Assent
300608:
Amends The Residential Tenancies Act to cap most rent increases at an annual guideline and set limited exceptions.

  • Limits rent increases during a tenancy to a yearly guideline set by the government
  • Guideline is based on Saskatchewan's Consumer Price Index change, published by August 31 each year
  • Landlords and tenants can agree to higher increases in exchange for capital upgrades or added services
  • Exempts hotels, motels, caretaker and employee units, and boarding house rooms from the rent cap
  • Exempts new buildings from rent control for 5 years after first occupancy
  • Allows landlords in buildings with 4 or more units to raise rent on a vacated unit up to the average rent of comparable units
  • Takes effect immediately upon receiving assent
300609:
Requires Saskatchewan's government to create a provincial strategy for preventing and managing wildfires.

  • Ministry of Corrections, Policing and Public Safety must establish a provincial wildfire management strategy
  • Ministry must provide public guidelines to raise awareness and knowledge about wildfires
  • Ministry must publish existing statistics on wildfire actions and risk factors
  • Ministry must promote collaboration and knowledge sharing across sectors and jurisdictions
  • Ministry must define best practices for preventing and fighting wildfires
  • Within 180 days, and yearly after, ministry must consult First Nations, Métis and municipal governments in Northern Saskatchewan, Canada, and wildfire experts
  • Ministry must report yearly on its progress on the wildfire strategy
300610:
Requires the Minister to publicly disclose online when a hospital emergency room only has virtual physician services and no in-person physician available.

  • Amends The Provincial Health Authority Act with a new section 7-6.1
  • Minister must publish this information via website or other electronic means
  • Notice must go out within one hour of the health authority approving virtual physician use
  • Ministry must use existing resources to cover any related costs
  • Expenses for publicizing this information cannot be paid from the General Revenue Fund
  • Takes effect immediately upon Assent
300611:
Requires the government to automatically send any provincial law that uses the Charter's notwithstanding clause to the Court of Appeal for review.

  • Amends The Constitutional Questions Act, 2012 to add a new referral requirement
  • Applies whenever a provincial Act declares it operates despite the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms under section 33
  • Requires the Lieutenant Governor in Council to refer the Act to the Court of Appeal
  • Referral must happen within 90 days after the Act comes into force
  • Court must give its opinion on whether the provision violates Charter section 2 or sections 7 to 15
  • Court must also say whether any violation is reasonable and justified under section 1 of the Charter
  • Takes effect immediately on royal assent
300612:
Requires the government to reject proposed 2026-2027 rate increases from SaskPower and SGI and freeze their rates at January 1, 2026 levels.

  • Minister of Crown Investments Corporation must disregard SaskPower's proposed 2026 and 2027 rate increase
  • Minister must also disregard SGI's proposed 2026 and 2027 rate increase
  • Rates for both corporations are frozen at their January 1, 2026 levels
  • Freeze continues until the Rate Review Panel gives recommendations to the Lieutenant Governor in Council
  • Starting one year after the Act takes effect, the Minister must publish a five-year rate increase projection annually
  • Projection must cover each subsidiary Crown corporation held by Crown Investments Corporation
  • The Act takes effect immediately upon receiving Assent
300613:
Amends The Saskatchewan Farm Security Act to make enforcement against illegal foreign farmland ownership mandatory and sharply increase penalties.

  • Requires the Minister, instead of the board, to act on illegal foreign farmland ownership cases
  • Raises one penalty amount from $1,000 to $1,000,000
  • Raises another penalty from $50,000 to $1,000,000
  • Increases a further penalty range from up to $500,000 to up to $10,000,000
  • Raises a separate penalty from $10,000 to up to $10,000,000
  • Removes certain existing exceptions or limits by repealing subsections 93(4) and 93.1(3)
  • Allows courts to order that net proceeds from a forced land sale be forfeited to the Crown
300614:
Bans physicians from charging patients extra fees or access fees for insured medical services in Saskatchewan.

  • Defines 'access fees' as extra charges for faster, preferred or exclusive access to insured services
  • States the Act's purpose is to prohibit private payment for insured health services
  • Prohibits physicians from charging or collecting any amount beyond government benefits for insured services
  • Blocks physicians from receiving government payment if they know a patient was charged an access fee
  • Allows charging for non-insured goods or services needed before an insured service, if not otherwise banned
  • Sets escalating penalties: warning, referral to the College of Physicians and Surgeons, then loss of eligibility for payment
  • Requires written notice, in plain language with signed acknowledgement, when a service is charged privately
300615:
Bans parking fees for cancer patients attending treatment at designated cancer care facilities operated by the Provincial Health Authority.

  • Amends The Provincial Health Authority Act by adding a new subsection
  • Prohibits charging parking fees to patients attending designated cancer treatment facilities
  • Applies to any health services entity or person operating such a facility
  • Covers facilities designated for cancer patient care under section 2-9
  • Comes into force immediately on Assent
300616:
Proclaims October of each year as Islamic Heritage Month in Saskatchewan.

  • Designates October as Islamic Heritage Month every year
  • Establishes the short title as The Islamic Heritage Month Act
  • Takes effect on the date it receives Assent
300617:
Requires the Minister to create a public registry listing family physicians and nurse practitioners currently accepting new patients.

  • Amends The Provincial Health Authority Act by adding a new section 7-6.1
  • Minister must publish a registry of family physicians and nurse practitioners accepting new patients
  • Registry must be accessible to the public through a website or other electronic means
  • Information must be made available within 3 months after the section takes effect
  • Ministry must use existing resources to administer and publicize the registry
  • Expenses for the registry cannot be paid from the General Revenue Fund
  • The Act comes into force on Assent
300618:
Prohibits the provincial health authority from contracting with a third party to set up an anonymous system for employees to report wrongdoing by other employees.

  • Amends The Provincial Health Authority Act
  • Bans the health authority from hiring outside companies to run anonymous employee reporting systems
  • Applies specifically to reports about wrongdoing by other employees
  • Takes effect on the date it receives Assent
300619:
Amends Saskatchewan's consumer protection law to ban businesses from charging consumers higher prices based on personalized algorithmic pricing.

  • Defines personalized algorithmic pricing, online retailers, online distributors and electronic shelf labelling systems
  • Bans charging a higher price at checkout than an electronic shelf label shows due to algorithmic pricing
  • Bans online retailers and distributors from using algorithms to raise prices charged to consumers
  • Treats use of personalized algorithmic pricing as a material fact that must be disclosed to consumers
  • Requires clear disclosure and active consumer consent before charging a higher price
  • Deems it an unfair business practice to charge higher prices via algorithmic pricing than offered to other consumers
  • Extends the time limit for prosecuting offences to two years after evidence comes to the director's knowledge
300620:
Voids restrictive covenants and exclusivity clauses that prevent land from being used for grocery stores or supermarkets.

  • Makes any new property control blocking grocery store or supermarket use void once the law takes effect
  • Voids existing restrictive covenants and exclusivity clauses unless the Minister specifically exempts them
  • Lets the Minister exempt pre-existing clauses only if they don't unduly hurt competition and serve the public interest
  • Exempts government, municipal, zoning-based, and building-scheme restrictions from the ban
  • Automatically removes exclusivity clauses that block supermarket use when held by someone other than a supermarket owner or related person
  • Defines grocery stores as at least 280 square metres and supermarkets as at least 929 square metres
  • Allows the government to make further regulations defining terms and exempting certain classes of clauses
300621:
Requires bidders on large public works projects over $50,000,000 to report on local job creation and community benefits, and prioritizes hiring Saskatchewan residents.

  • Defines community benefit as social, economic or environmental gains from a project, including local jobs and training
  • Requires bidders on public works over $50,000,000 to report expected community benefits before contracts are awarded
  • Requires bidders to report expected hours worked by Saskatchewan residents, unionized employees, apprentices and Indigenous persons
  • Requires bidders to report expected hours worked by other Canadian residents and non-Canadian residents
  • Requires the Minister to consider community benefits and worker categories when selecting winning bids
  • Requires contractors to prioritize hiring Saskatchewan residents, unionized employees, apprentices and Indigenous persons during construction
  • Requires monthly public reports on community benefits and actual hours worked, plus annual reporting by the Minister
300622:
Prohibits the provincial health authority from increasing board members' pay while contract negotiations with healthcare worker unions are ongoing.

  • Amends The Provincial Health Authority Act
  • Adds a new rule to section 3-9
  • Blocks the health authority from raising member remuneration during active union negotiations
  • Applies specifically to negotiations over healthcare worker contracts
  • Takes effect immediately upon Assent
300624:
Exempts children's clothing and various grocery store foods from provincial sales tax.

  • Removes provincial sales tax on clothing for children under age 16
  • Exempts ready-to-eat grocery meals like rotisserie chickens, chili and soup from tax
  • Exempts pre-packaged salads, sandwiches and wraps from provincial sales tax
  • Exempts mixed and salted nuts, muffins, granola and protein bars from tax
  • Exempts fruit juices and yogurt drinks from provincial sales tax
  • Exempts cheese, meat, fruit and vegetable platters from provincial sales tax
  • Allows the Lieutenant Governor in Council to add more exempt foods by regulation
300625:
Amends the Members' Conflict of Interest Act to define apparent conflicts of interest and require fuller disclosure of members' private business holdings.

  • Adds a new definition of apparent conflict of interest based on reasonable public perception
  • Applies when a reasonably well-informed person could think a member's private interest affected their official duties
  • Requires members to disclose detailed descriptions of businesses held by private or holding companies they control
  • Extends this disclosure duty to businesses controlled by the member's family members
  • Requires listing both the operating name and legal name of such businesses
  • Takes effect immediately upon receiving Assent
300626:
Amends The Lobbyists Act to require more detailed disclosure of lobbying activities and to ban public office holders from accepting gifts from lobbyists.

  • Defines 'communicate' broadly to include emails, phone calls, and in-person or remote meetings
  • Defines 'gift' to match The Members' Conflict of Interest Act definition
  • Removes an exemption for non-profits with fewer than 5 employees from certain provisions
  • Removes the exemption for lobbying activity under 30 hours annually from registration requirements
  • Requires disclosure of all political financial contributions by organizations employing in-house or consultant lobbyists since the last election writ
  • Requires lobbyists to file monthly activity logs detailing who they lobbied, on what topics, and how they communicated
  • Bans public office holders from accepting gifts from lobbyists, except MLAs following conflict of interest rules
300628:
Amends Saskatchewan's freedom of information law to require disclosure of public interest information and strengthen the process for appealing and enforcing information commissioner recommendations.

  • Allows officials to waive or reduce information request fees if the applicant cannot afford them or the record is in the public interest
  • Creates a new duty to disclose, without delay, information about risks of significant harm to environment, health or safety
  • Requires disclosure of any other information that is clearly in the public interest, overriding other exemptions in the Act
  • Requires notice to affected third parties and the commissioner before such public interest disclosures, when practicable
  • Removes solicitor-client and other legal privilege protections when the commissioner requests records
  • Gives heads of public bodies 10 days to respond in writing to commissioner recommendations, or be deemed to agree
  • Lets the commissioner file enforceable court orders when a public body fails to comply with recommendations
300629:
Amends child and family services law to guide disclosure decisions on historical records and require preservation of documents related to residential schools and the sixties scoop.

  • Requires the Minister to consider specific factors when deciding whether to disclose information
  • Factors include requests by family about a deceased child's death or injury in care
  • Considers whether disclosure relates to sixties scoop or residential school records
  • Considers whether disclosure supports truth and reconciliation goals
  • Considers whether disclosure would help improve the child and family services system
  • Requires written reasons if the Minister refuses to release requested information
  • Requires preservation of records on Indigenous children in residential schools, day schools, or the sixties scoop
300630:
Requires public disclosure and independent review of contracts where public money funds privately delivered health services in Saskatchewan.

  • Creates a public online registry listing details of contracts for private health services funded with public money
  • Applies to private surgical clinics, diagnostic labs, addictions treatment, agency nursing, long-term care and P3 health projects
  • Requires contract details like value, duration and performance measures to be published within 30 days of signing
  • Requires full contract text be public, with limited redactions for personal or safety information
  • Bars withholding contract values, payment structures, staffing rates, and termination terms from the public
  • Requires the Provincial Auditor to review value-for-money on contracts over $10 million and all P3 health deals
  • Requires an annual government report on spending, staffing, wait times, and outcomes for contracted health services
